lesson.title: Wie geht's? — How goes it?
lesson.subtitle: Greetings and small-talk idioms as archaic English survivals

hook.title: The Frozen Sentences
hook.content: Germans greet each other in sentences English used to say. Wie geht's? = 'How goes it?' — the question your great-great-grandparents asked. Es geht mir gut = 'It goes to-me well' — the dative experiencer answering. Auf Wiedersehen = 'until re-seeing' — a farewell that refuses to be final (on the phone: Auf Wiederhören, 'until re-hearing'!). Guten Morgen = 'good morning' — word for word. And the small talk runs the same way: Was machst du? = 'What make you?' — no do-support, the archaic flip. German small talk is a museum of Early Modern English where all the exhibits still work.

footnotes.title: Tschüss, the Sailor's Farewell
footnotes.content: The informal Tschüss has a wild history: Hanseatic sailors bent French adieu ('to God') into Low German adjüs, which wore down to Tschüss. The casual goodbye carries a thousand years of sea trade and a French blessing inside it.

pattern.title: The Small-Talk Shelf
pattern.content: Greeting: Guten Morgen / Guten Tag / Guten Abend — the good-morning formula, word for word. Asking: Wie geht's? / Wie geht es dir? (how goes it TO YOU — the dative dir from topic 20). Answering: Es geht mir gut / schlecht (it goes to-me well/badly) or Danke, gut! Returning: Und dir? (and to-thee?). The dative feeling set joins in: Mir ist kalt (I am cold — to-me), Mir ist langweilig (I am bored — to-me it is boring). The farewell: Tschüss! (casual), Auf Wiedersehen (formal — until re-seeing). Every line is archaic English with German endings.
pattern.linguist_note: The 's in Wie geht's is a contraction of es: Wie geht es? → Wie geht's? English once made the identical contraction — 'how goes't?' appears in Shakespeare. The apostrophe is the same grammatical event.

exercises.prompt: The small-talk shelf — match each greeting with its literal reading:
exercises.target_answer: Wie geht's?, Es geht mir gut, Auf Wiedersehen, Guten Tag, Es geht mir schlecht, Die Leute sind lustig
exercises.meaning: how are you, I'm fine, goodbye, hello
exercises.explanation: Every greeting is an English sentence your language retired — German still runs them daily.

exercises.prompt: Why 'Es geht MIR gut' and not 'Es geht mich gut'?
options: The experiencer takes the dative — it goes well TO ME
mich is a spelling error here
exercises.target_answer: The experiencer takes the dative — it goes well TO ME
exercises.meaning: The dative of experience from topic 20
exercises.explanation: Going-well happens TO you: mir. The same case as methinks and mir ist kalt. Bist du fertig? — fertig (ready, journey-fared) asks it with sein.

exercises.prompt: On the phone, Germans say 'Auf Wiederhören'. Why hören?
options: Until re-HEARING — you hear, not see, on the phone
exercises.target_answer: Until re-HEARING — you hear, not see, on the phone
exercises.explanation: The farewell describes the exact sense in play: seeing in person, hearing on the phone. German calques reality.

exercises.prompt: Which Shakespearean phrase answers 'Wie geht es dir?' word for word?
exercises.meaning: How goes it? ↔ Wie geht es dir?
exercises.explanation: Same question, same verb-first form — plus the dative dir (to-thee) English dropped. The answers fill the feeling fridge: glücklich, krank, satt, Hunger. Und der Himmel? — the small-talk weather report: der Himmel ist grau, aber der Mensch ist glücklich.

exercises.prompt: Assemble a full small-talk exchange: 'How are you? — Thanks, good! And you?'
exercises.target_answer: Wie geht's Danke gut und dir
exercises.meaning: How goes it? — Thanks, well! And thee?

vocab_hints.note: im Urlaub — the question small talk always reaches for: Wie war der Urlaub am Meer? How was the holiday at the sea? The Urlaub is the reason you two are talking at all.

exercises.explanation: The whole dance in six words: the dative question, the dative thanks, the dative return — Und dir? (and to-thee?). Then the follow-up every German small talk turns to: Wie war der Urlaub? — how was the holiday?

summary.outcome: Run a full German small-talk exchange and hear the archaic English inside it.

use_example.german: Wie geht's? — Danke, gut! Und dir?
use_example.english: How goes it? — Thanks, well! And thee?

summary.takeaway: The greetings are frozen English sentences: How goes it, until re-seeing, good day — with the dative doing the pointing.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Mir ist kalt — the dative feelings: cold, boredom, and sorrow all happen TO you.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Wie geht's? — How goes it? (How goes it? — Thanks, well! And thee):
twist.target_answer: Wie geht's Danke gut und dir
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wie geht's Danke gut und dir" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Wie geht's? — How goes it? without relying on short-term echo.

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

danken.etymology_derivation: Danke is an ellipsis of "[Ich] danke [dir/Ihnen]".

schlecht.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *slihtaz 'smooth, level' — Wiktionary: cognate with English slight. [wiktionary]

fertig.etymology_derivation: From Old High German fartig, literally journey-ready, from fart (journey), the ancestor of modern Fahrt; the root belongs with the Germanic travel word behind English fare, and Dutch has the parallel vaardig. [wiktionary]

lustig.etymology_derivation: Lust (desire, joy) plus -ig; Lust is the exact cognate of English lust, from Proto-Germanic *lustuz, though in German the sexual shade is weak and the word still means plain pleasure, as in Lust haben. [wiktionary]

hunger.context_translation: I have great hunger / I am very hungry.

krank.context_phrase: Ich bin krank und bleibe zu Hause.
krank.context_translation: I am sick and staying home.
krank.etymology_derivation: Old sense 'crooked, weak' — Wiktionary: cognate with English crank. [wiktionary]

satt.etymology_derivation: From Old High German sat, Proto-Germanic *sadaz, meaning sated or full; the exact cognate is English sad, which originally meant sated before it drifted to its modern sorrowful sense. [wiktionary]

glücklich.etymology_derivation: Glück (luck) + -lich; Wiktionary: 'Compare English luck' — a relative via Dutch. [wiktionary]

leute.context_translation: Many people are waiting at the station.
leute.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *liudiz, kin to the Old English leode (men, people); German keeps the plural-only collective with the standard article die Leute. [wiktionary]

himmel.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *himil — the same Germanic line as English heaven's root family. [wiktionary]

mensch.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *manniskaz 'human', built on Mann — English mannish is the cognate form. [wiktionary]

urlaub.context_phrase: Ich fahre im Urlaub nach Italien.
urlaub.context_translation: I go to Italy on vacation.
urlaub.etymology_derivation: Middle High German urloup 'permission to be away', kin to erlauben — cognate with English leave. [wiktionary]

meer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German meri, from Proto-West Germanic *mari. English mere is the listed cognate, and Latin mare is cognate through Indo-European. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
